results.author: Artem Bukhkalov
highlights:
Renting is the other way in, and it is the market we measure. At the Compute Census index of 6 Nov 2026, the median on-demand price of an H100 80GB is $3.90 per GPU-hour, the cheapest accepted offer is $1.30 and the most expensive list price is $12.29. A published 12-month reserved rate stands at $3.26.

...

Against 1 Oct 2025, the H100 median has moved +100%. ... Through 2024 and 2025, rental prices fell as new capacity came online and Blackwell systems began shipping. AWS cut on-demand prices for its P5 H100 instances by 44 percent from 1 June 2025, with savings plans cut by up to 45 percent. Many observers read that as the start of a long slide.

The slide stopped. SemiAnalysis reported in April 2026 that on-demand capacity was sold out and that H100 contracts were being renewed at the same rates signed two to three years earlier, some for four years through 2028. Its one-year H100 contract index rose from $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026. Providers then raised list prices: Nebius lifted its on-demand H100 rate to $4.50 per GPU-hour from 1 October 2026, about 17 percent higher, its second increase in three months according to Silicon UK. AWS now lists Capacity Blocks for its eight-GPU H100 instance at $47.757 per instance-hour, or $5.970 per GPU-hour.

Nebius raised H100 prices 17% and H200 prices 20% on September 17, effective October 1. H100 and H200 are two of the GPUs most teams rent for LLM training and inference. If you had an instance running under the old contract, the new rate applies to it now, not at renewal.

You did not choose that new rate. A fixed-term contract works like this: the provider sets a new price, and every running instance inherits it on the provider's schedule. Per-minute billing works differently. You pay whatever rate is posted right now, for the minutes you actually use, and nothing carries forward past that.

On Spheron, that means:

- You see the live rate before every deployment, not on an annual renewal notice.
- You can move a workload to a different GPU or provider the same day if a better rate shows up elsewhere.
- Reserved pricing still exists if you want a fixed rate locked in. On-demand just stays the default instead of something you have to opt into.

As of October 6, 2026, on-demand H100 starts at $2.01/hr on the marketplace, and spot H200 starts at $3.31/hr. Spot means the rate for using capacity that is free right now, and it runs below the on-demand rate. These are live marketplace numbers and can vary by region.

A fixed-term contract can raise your rate without warning. Check current on-demand and spot rates on the marketplace before your next renewal

results.title: Learnings from tracking GPU and token prices for fun - DEV Community
results.author: Paul Piper
highlights:
Learnings from tracking GPU and token prices for fun - DEV Community
Paul Piper
Posted on Oct 20 • Originally published at madppiper.substack.com
# Learnings from tracking GPU and token prices for fun
Part of my job, and honestly part of my hobby, is watching prices. Not all of them, of course (I mean, what a lunatic must you be), but specific ones: GPU and inference endpoints. A while back I noticed that they differ immensely across providers, so I built a tool. Smart Inference, the router Jenni and I run, reads the price of GPU rentals and LLM tokens from a list of providers around the clock and sends each request to the cheapest healthy option. Since April it has kept every price it ever saw, which by now is roughly 11 million GPU price points and 3.3 million token prices.
I was wondering if my own data would support my theory that there is “overcapacity in the market”. Alas, that is not really what it shows.
I start in June, because before that we had too few providers to say much. From June to October, the median hourly price of the GPUs everybody wants went up:
* H100, on-demand: 3.25 to 3.89 dollars (+20%)
* H200, on-demand: 4.00 to 5.02 dollars (+25%)
* B200, on-demand: 6.11 to 7.42 dollars (+21%)
* B200, spot: 2.14 to 3.78 dollars (+77%)
Meanwhile, even the spot pricing options jumped: H100 in June was offered at a low of 1.04 an hour, and was bumped to 1.81 in October. This fits the overall market trend.
There is one exception, however and that is older hardware: An A100 on spot went from 1.07 to 0.88 an hour back in July and has sat there ever since. So it looks like people are fighting over newer hardware and perhaps if you want to really make a bargain right now, those can be a better choice.
Then I looked at the token side (my inference endpoints) and that’s where it got weird: Across all providers that serve the same model, the median price per million input tokens shifted a lot. DeepSeek V4 was at 1.30 dollars until July and is selling for 0.30 now, about 77% less. GLM-5 went from 1.00 in May to 0.15 in October. Output tokens fell almost as hard (DeepSeek V4: 2.60 down to 1.20, GLM-5: 3.20 to 0.50).
So a steep price drop, even though the models are unchanged and hardware got more expensive. To be fair, not everything got cheaper. Kimi K2.6 and GLM-4.7 stayed roughly the same, and gpt-oss-120b even went up a little at the median. But the big new open models, the ones people actually switch to, lost three quarters of their price or more within a few months of launch.
All in all, hardware got about 20% more expensive and inference got 80% cheaper. Makes no sense, but okay…
I have some theories why that may be: sometimes models are subsidized, other times providers get better at running the models (quantization is a thing) and maybe, just maybe older models are downgraded to lower specs (which could also have an impact on performance).
Theories aside, what it shows, however, is that my own idea that “the market is producing vast overcapacity for AI” is not really the case. At least not according to the data. If that were the case, my own pricing table, which also features “spot pricing”, should get cheaper over time, not more expensive. For current hardware it looks more like the opposite, the GPUs get pricier. It also means that sometimes model providers are eating the costs.
That matters more than you may think: it means that at least for now, it is more expensive to run your own GPU than it is to build on inference infrastructure. If token prices drop faster than GPU prices, renting your own GPU stops making sense for most workloads, and buying tokens from whoever is cheapest this week wins. Six months ago I would have told you that self-hosting on spot GPUs was the smart move for steady traffic. Today, for the big open models, I would check the token price first.
Before I finish this, you should be aware that this observation is only based on our own data: every monthly median comes from two to seven providers, the mix changes from month to month as we onboard additional ones. So even though the data points are complete, we are only comparing a small subset of providers.
Anyway, I love to be proven wrong, so I will keep checking up on the market in the near future. I will keep you posted…

results.title: Why do two teams running the same 70B model end up with completely different hourly bills? | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
Most run inference on one GPU type for everything. That is simple to manage, but it wastes money.

...

Prefill reads your prompt and needs raw compute. Decode writes the answer one token at a time and needs memory bandwidth more than math. Bandwidth is how fast a GPU moves data in and out of memory. On a 70B model, decode takes up about 80% of the total time a request spends on the GPU.

Match each phase to the GPU built for it:

- Send prefill to H100, where raw compute wins
- Send decode to L40S, where you pay less per unit of bandwidth
- Run them together as one rig: 1x H100 plus 2x L40S

That rig costs $4.01/hr. Four H100s cost $10.28/hr for the same job, a 61% cut in hourly rig cost. Cost per million tokens falls from $0.89 to $0.46, roughly a 48% reduction.

There is a catch. L40S runs prefill 2.7 times slower than H100, and the saving only holds because prefill is the smaller slice of the clock. Get the prefill-to-decode ratio wrong and the saving shrinks.
